The paper explores the relationship between individual and collective inference in multi-agent Bayesian systems.
The authors demonstrate an equivalence between collective active inference and spin glass systems.
A spin glass system is a type of statistical physics model that exhibits complex behavior.
Active inference is a Bayesian inference framework that involves both perception and action.
Glauber dynamics is an algorithm for sampling from the stationary distribution of a spin glass system.
The probability of taking a particular action can be expressed in terms of the posterior over latent states z.
The likelihood and prior precisions determine the steepness and horizontal shift of the logistic function.
The approximate posterior over control states is a Bernoulli distribution with parameter φ.
The authors supplement each agent's current generative model with an extra random variable that corresponds to control states.
The authors perform active inference with respect to an augmented generative model.
The approximate posterior over control states simplifies to the state posterior when the predictive generative model is used.
The paper highlights the importance of considering both individual and collective inference in multi-agent systems.
The authors use a specific type of spin glass model, the Ising model, to demonstrate the equivalence between collective active inference and spin glass systems.
The Ising model is a type of spin glass model that exhibits phase transitions and emergent phenomena.
The authors show that the parameters of individual generative models can be related to the local energy difference and global energy of the system.
The authors use a Gibbs law or Boltzmann distribution to relate the global energy to the stationary probability distribution of the system.
The authors use a stochastic update rule based on the energy difference between configurations to update each spin in the system.
The authors use a Bernoulli distribution to parameterize the likelihood and prior distributions in the generative model.
The authors use a logistic function to represent the posterior belief over the hidden spin state.
The authors use a variational Bayesian inference framework to optimize the approximate posterior over control states.
